idea.body: Some tangled trig expressions are secretly the same thing in disguise. The Pythagorean identity sin^2(x) + cos^2(x) = 1 rearranges into 1 + tan^2(x) = sec^2(x) and 1 + cot^2(x) = csc^2(x). The sum formula sin(a + b) = sin(a) cos(b) + cos(a) sin(b) gives exact values at angles like 75 degrees. Setting a = b = x gives the double angle formulas, sin(2x) = 2 sin(x) cos(x) and cos(2x) = 1 - 2 sin^2(x). To prove an identity, start from one side and use these tools, one step at a time, until it matches the other side. For example, sin(x) + sin(x) cot^2(x) factors to sin(x)(1 + cot^2(x)), which is sin(x) times csc^2(x), which is csc(x): the two sides really are equal.

steps: Write sec(x) as 1/cos(x), using the reciprocal identity.
The left side becomes cos(x) times 1/cos(x).
The left side equals 1, matching the right side.

ways.name: Rewrite in sine and cosine
ways.when: Use this first whenever an identity mixes tangent, cotangent, secant or cosecant.
steps: Rewrite tan(x) as sin(x)/cos(x), using the quotient identity.
The left side becomes (sin(x)/cos(x)) times cos(x).
The cos(x) terms cancel, leaving sin(x), which matches the right side.
ways.trap: Forgetting the quotient identity and leaving tan(x) unrewritten.

ways.name: The Pythagorean identity substitution
ways.when: Use this when an expression has 1 minus cos^2 or 1 minus sin^2 hiding inside it.
steps: The Pythagorean identity sin^2(x) + cos^2(x) = 1 rearranges to 1 - cos^2(x) = sin^2(x).
One factor of sin(x) cancels, leaving sin(x).
ways.trap: Expanding 1 - cos^2(x) some other way instead of spotting the Pythagorean pattern.
